pages.title: Start here: how this workspace runs

text.text: A ten-minute tour of how the company's work flows through this workspace. Share it with the dispatcher, the office manager and each technician.
What lives where
Customers
: homes, landlords and businesses, with what they have been billed, what they still owe, open calls, and whether they are on a plan.
Equipment
: every furnace, heat pump, AC, boiler and mini-split you look after, with make, model, serial, install year, filter size, refrigerant, warranty and condition.
Service calls
: every visit, linked to the customer and the unit, with the tech, the date, the price and the margin.
Maintenance agreements
: who is on a plan, what they paid, visits left, and when it renews.
Parts and stock
: what is on the trucks and shelves and what needs ordering.
Invoices
: what is billed, paid and late.
A call from phone to paid
The call comes in. The dispatcher adds a service call on the board (or the customer uses the Request form) as
New request
, picks the unit, and sets the priority.
The dispatcher books the lead tech and a date, and moves it to
Scheduled
. A tech can press
Assign to me
to take a call; it then shows in their Mine list.
On site the tech works the job sheet, enters parts and hours, and updates the unit's condition.
Mark done
closes the call and stamps the date.
The office sends the invoice. If it goes past due, set it to
Overdue
: the customer's Awaiting payment counts sent and overdue together.
Mark paid
stamps the payment date.
Your rhythm
Every morning: Dashboard, then overdue calls, then the Awaiting payment list
Every Monday: Renewing in 30 days, and book plan visits
Every Friday: truck and shelf count
Every month: callbacks, thin margins, and units marked Replace soon (your replacement leads)
Making it yours

Rename the plans and work types to your own, add your trucks, and delete the sample customers after you have added a dozen of your own. Type in any cell, drag cards between columns; every total updates by itself.
Open calls, money in and money owed at a glance. Anything under Overdue needs a phone call today.
Overdue service calls
My service calls
Overdue invoices
Awaiting payment (sent and overdue)
Plans renewing in the next 30 days
Units to replace soon
A good service call is predictable: the customer knows when you are coming, the tech knows the equipment before arriving, and the invoice goes out before the truck leaves the driveway.
Before the truck rolls
Open the call and check the
Unit
it is linked to. Model, serial, age, filter size and refrigerant are on that unit's card. If the unit is not there yet, the tech adds it on site.
Look at the unit's earlier service calls. A second igniter in three weeks is not bad luck; it is a wiring or gas pressure problem, and it should go to your most senior tech.
Load the right filter and the common failures for that make: igniter, flame sensor, capacitor, contactor.
Text the customer the tech's name and a two-hour window, then a heads-up thirty minutes out.
On site, every call
Shoe covers on, drop cloth under the work area
Ask the customer what they noticed, when it started, and what they already tried
Check the thermostat and the filter first; a clogged filter causes more no-heat calls than any part
Test before replacing: amp draw, capacitor value, temperature split, gas pressure, flue draft
Carbon monoxide reading at the supply register and around the furnace on every gas call
Show the customer the failed part and the reading that proved it
Give a price before the repair; offer the options (repair, repair plus plan, replace)
Pricing
Price repairs from a flat-rate book so two techs never quote the same job differently. Put real parts cost and hours on the call so the
Margin
shows the truth; anything under twenty percent shows as Thin. Plan members get their discount on parts, and their tune-up visits are priced at zero because the agreement already paid for them.
No-heat emergencies in winter

When it is below freezing, a no-heat call jumps the queue. Ask about elderly people, infants or pets in the home, and about pipes in outside walls. If the part is not on the truck, leave portable heaters and book the return the same day. Mark the call
Emergency
so the board shows it in red.
Example

A small restaurant calls at opening: the rooftop unit blows warm. The dispatcher sees from the unit card it is a 2015 packaged unit on R-410A that was serviced last quarter. Ilse finds a weak start capacitor and a pitted contactor, replaces both from the truck, and the kitchen is cool before lunch. She enters 3 hours and the part costs, presses
Mark done
, and the office sends the invoice that afternoon.
Callbacks
If you return to fix your own work, tick
Callback
on the new call and do not bill it. Review callbacks every month with the techs: each one costs a truck, a tech and a customer's trust.
Maintenance agreements smooth out the year. They fill the slow weeks in spring and fall, they keep equipment running longer, and plan members are the first to call you when it is time to replace.
What a plan includes here
Comfort Club
: a heating check in the fall and a cooling check in the spring, priority booking, no after-hours surcharge.
Comfort Club Plus
: the same, plus 15 percent off repair parts and one free filter change between visits.
Commercial quarterly
: four visits a year for rooftop units and boilers, with filters and belts included.
Set your own names and prices in the Plan column; the board updates with them.
Selling a plan
Offer it on every repair call, after the repair, when the customer has seen what a neglected unit costs.
Keep it to one sentence: "For the price of one repair a year, we look after it twice and you jump the queue."
Add the agreement with a start date and a renewal date one year out. Set
Visits left this year
to the number of visits in the plan.
Running the visits
At the start of each season, open
Renewing in 30 days
and the agreements board, and book every member who still has a visit left.
Book plan visits as service calls with work type
Maintenance plan visit
, linked to the unit.
After each visit, take one off Visits left.
The plan visit checklist
Replace or wash the filter, note its size on the unit card
Clean the condenser coil and check the condensate drain
Test capacitors, contactors and blower amps
Gas: check burners, igniter, flame sensor, heat exchanger and flue; carbon monoxide test
Heat pump: check defrost and refrigerant pressures against the label
Set the unit's
Condition
to Good, Watch or Replace soon, and tell the customer why
Renewals
A plan that lapses is very hard to win back. Work the
Renewing in 30 days

list every week: call or text, take the card, and push the renewal date out one year. If the customer says no, set the status to Cancelled and write the reason on the agreement, so you can see why plans are lost.
Example

In early September the service manager opens the renewals list: six agreements renew in the next month. He books fall visits for the four who still have one left and calls the two that are due. One renews on the phone; the other moved away, so he marks it Cancelled with that note.
The difference between a one-trip repair and a two-trip repair is usually a ten-dollar part. Count weekly, reorder early, and keep the common failures on every truck.
The weekly count
Every Friday afternoon the techs count their trucks; the office counts the shop shelves.
Type the real count into
On hand
and set
Last counted
to the day.
Sort by
Reorder?
and send one order per supplier before the weekend so parts are on will-call Monday morning.
What every service truck carries
Electrical: run capacitors in the common sizes, contactors, a universal control board, fuses
Heating: hot surface igniters, flame sensors, pressure switches, inducer motor for your most common make
Cooling: condensate pumps, float switches, a recovery machine and refrigerant for the systems you service
Filters in the five sizes you see most often (check the Filter size column on Equipment to find them)
Thermostat, wire, and a manometer, a combustion analyzer and a CO meter
Refrigerant

Track refrigerant by the cylinder and know which systems use which. Older systems on retired refrigerants are getting expensive to recharge: when the Equipment list shows one in Watch or Replace soon, offer a replacement estimate before the next leak, not after.
Setting reorder points

Look at what you used in the last two weeks and add a safety amount for a cold snap. Igniters and capacitors fail in waves on the first hot or cold week of the season, so raise those points a month before it.
Warranty parts
When a failed part is under warranty, keep it in a tagged bag with the unit's serial number and the date. The Equipment card shows the warranty date; claims are usually refused without the old part.
Checklist when a part runs out on a job
Call the dispatcher before leaving the site
Check whether another truck nearby has it
Put the call On hold with the part named in the notes
Book the return as soon as the part arrives, and tell the customer when
Example

On Friday Marcus counts flame sensors: three left, reorder point five. The row shows Reorder. The office adds six to the Badger Furnace Parts order. The first cold weekend brings four short-cycling furnaces, and every one is fixed on the first trip.
